You wrote section 1 of 6, "What the framework is for", of the report "AI readiness of federal statistical publishers: what one measurement shows". It was checked, and it comes back to you once with the notes below. Rewrite the whole section so that the notes no longer apply, keeping its argument and keeping every fact you can keep under the rules.

WHAT THIS SECTION MUST DO: State what the framework is for: whether the public, and the tools the public now uses to find and read data (search engines, AI assistants and the programs behind them), can reach, understand and use the data the public paid for. Say how the framework is built (its criteria and indicators) and why reaching data is a distinct problem from publishing it, using the prior-art claims. Do not report any measurement result here.

THE SECTION AS IT STANDS (markers in place)
The framework exists to rate and score, quantitatively and qualitatively, whether the public and the tools the public now uses can reach, understand and use the data they paid for [c:CL-085]. The Department of Commerce has set a neighbouring target in its guidance glossary, which defines AI-ready data as data that is not just machine-readable but machine-understandable, enriched with contextual metadata and organized in interpretable standard formats for use by AI systems [c:CL-085]. That glossary belongs to guidance written by the Department's Data Governance Board, not to a Department-wide regulation, and read beside the framework's own statement it describes the data, whereas the framework asks whether people and their tools can get to the data and use it [c:CL-085].

Publishing data and reaching it are separate problems, because each step between a released file and its use can fail on its own [c:CL-078]. Wilkinson and colleagues, setting out the FAIR principles, describe a machine agent that must identify an object, judge it useful, judge it usable with respect to licence, consent and access, and then act, so a machine can complete one step and fail the next [c:CL-078]. Structured metadata on a page therefore does not by itself make data usable by machines, since discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use are each required [c:CL-078]. Fitness for use is also the term federal statistical guidance uses for data quality, defined there as fitness for a user's own needs [c:CL-078]. For example, figures released in aggregated spreadsheets laid out for presentation are not machine-usable even when published, because a format that machines cannot read places severe limits on what the data can be used for [c:CL-086].

Writing for machine readers already has a named discipline, generative engine optimization, which its originators present as the successor to search engine optimization [c:CL-080]. Those machine readers face a further barrier, because publishers increasingly restrict AI crawlers and the public's access to data through AI tools depends on those restrictions [c:CL-081]. The cost of a restriction falls on the public, since OpenAI states that sites opted out of its search crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, and Anthropic warns that blocking its search crawler may reduce a site's visibility and accuracy in user search results [c:CL-081].

The framework's structure starts from the 4 criteria USAFacts set out, that data be accessible, understandable, accurate and open, and adds 3 more, for 7 criteria in all [c:CL-047]. Below the criteria, the framework record holds 50 indicators, of which 48 are in the framework and 2 are candidates [c:CL-046]. Those 2 candidates, the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, enter no framework count until the framework's operator adopts them [c:CL-046].

REGISTER
- Technical and readable. The reader is a federal statistician or a manager at a statistical agency: expert in statistics, not in web crawling or AI.
- Each paragraph carries one thought, stated in its first sentence (the topic sentence); the rest of the paragraph develops it.
- In each sentence, put what the reader already knows first and what is new last, where the stress falls (Gopen and Swan, "The Science of Scientific Writing", 1990).
- Wherever the logic turns (a contrast, a cause, a consequence, an example), say so with a connective word: but, so, because, therefore, for example, however.
- Write whole sentences with a finite verb. Do not follow a long sentence with a short fragment or a short qualifying sentence (for example "Not a browser." or "Only the public pages."); fold the qualification into the sentence it qualifies. This pattern is measured and a section that repeats it fails.
- Vary sentence length naturally. Do not repeat a phrase you have already used; find the plain word for each thing and use it once where once is enough.
- Never use the em dash or the en dash. Never use these words: load-bearing, load bearing, hallucinate (or any form of it; say confabulate), delve, testament. Do not cite Gartner.
- Plain names, no codes. Name a statistical body by its name (the NAMES table gives it), never by a code such as CENSUS or BLS. Name a check by what it tests (for example "the check for a machine-readable licence"), never by a letter-and-number code such as D1 or B2. Do not use task codes, decision numbers, file names, file paths, field names in backticks, or words like harness, pipeline, record node, leg, route, cycle id; call the measuring client "the scanner". The one identifier you may write is the name of the measurement cycle, scan_2026-10-07_composite_d, at most once in the whole report, where the section says what was measured.
- Do not use Markdown formatting inside sentences: no bold, no italics, no backticks, no bullet lists.

FACTS
- Every fact you state must come from the CLAIMS below. Do not use anything you know from elsewhere, even if you are sure it is true. FRAMING text, if any, tells you what the work is for; it is not a source of facts, and a fact taken from it that no claim states will be cut.
- A sentence that states a fact ends with the ids of the claims that support every part of it, written as [c:CL-035] or [c:CL-035, CL-036], placed before the final full stop. A sentence with no fact in it (a transition, a statement of what the section does) has no marker.
- Write every number exactly as a claim states it, in digits, with its thousands separator (1,055, not 1055 or one thousand and fifty-five). Do not compute a new number (no sums, differences, percentages or ratios that no claim states). A number that is not in a claim the sentence cites will be cut.
- Do not overstate. A claim that says "at most", "a bound, not a value", "notional", "not established" or "candidate" keeps that qualification in your sentence.
- A sentence that the claims do not support will be cut, not repaired, and the argument will have a hole where it was.
